Virgin Atlantic made headlines on November 28, 2023, when its large passenger plane, powered by used cooking oil, completed a transatlantic flight from London to New York. This remarkable event, though indicating a(n) [[1]] fossil fuels, sparked debate on the benefits of using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
SAF refers to a type of aviation fuel that is made from renewable starting materials, such as used cooking oils and food waste. Burning SAF still emits CO₂ because it is chemically identical to traditional jet fuel, but supporters argue that when the entire [[2]] of SAF is considered, the CO₂ emissions can be balanced out. In other words, the amount of carbon emissions generated when SAF is burned is roughly [[3]] the amount reduced during the generation of SAF.
However, SAF can be derived from a wide range of materials, some of which may be harmful to the environment. Critics argue that the airline is prematurely touting its environmental benefits. For example, the practice of energy growing crops, or crops [[4]] for generating renewable energy rather than food, could lead to deforestation and habitat loss. Land, the second largest carbon store, can capture carbon emissions, and reduced land availability means less are [[5]], resulting in increased CO₂ levels on earth.
The debate continues whether SAF could be the solution to airplane pollution.
